desc: The Atomic Energy Commission was created by the Atomic Energy Act of 1946 and took statutory title to everything the Manhattan Engineer District had held: all fissionable material, all atomic weapons and parts, and all processes and technical information behind them. It ran the born-secret information regime, under which data in defined categories is classified by operation of statute and declassified only by an affirmative act of the Commission, and it gated every contractor employee's access behind an FBI investigation and a Commission determination. Its Division of Military Application was established in the founding statute and directed by a serving officer of the armed forces. The Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 abolished it and vested its functions in ERDA, from which they passed to the Department of Energy. Four guests across four Michels lead maps place the Commission at a custody point for recovered material; nothing in either statute or in the National Archives record group description says anything about recovered material, and the node carries the statute rather than the testimony.

dossier.denialPosture: The Commission is not recorded on this board as having denied anything, and no denial link touches this node in either direction. Its disclosure letter is the lowest on the map for a reason that is architectural rather than behavioural: a body operating a born-secret regime does not need to deny, because the statute withholds by default and release requires an affirmative act the Commission alone can take. The board's discipline on this node runs the same way. Guest testimony placing it at a custody point for recovered material is not carried as a claim, because the statute and the archival record say nothing to support it.
dossier.narrative:
The Commission is on this board for what its statute permits, not for what any witness says it did. Section 9(a) transferred to it 'All fissionable material; all atomic weapons and parts thereof' and, in the same list, 'Such other property owned by or in the custody or control of the Manhattan Engineer District or other Government agencies as the President may determine.' That second clause is a custody instrument with no subject-matter limit in it. Any account that has recovered material moving into federal custody in the late 1940s has to explain which authority received it, and this is the authority whose founding statute was drafted to receive whatever the President said it should receive.

The classification regime is the second half of the same argument. Restricted data under the 1946 Act is 'all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power, but shall not include any data which the Commission from time to time determines may be published without adversely affecting the common defense and security.' The default runs the opposite way from every executive-order system on this board: information is secret because of what it is about, and it becomes public only by an affirmative act. A Division of Military Application, statutorily directed by a member of the armed forces, sat inside this civilian body from the first day. Civilian control with a uniformed division and a self-executing secrecy rule is a specific architecture, and it is the one the board keeps pointing at.

The geography closes the case for placement. CIA's own overhead reconnaissance history records that after the April 1955 overflight, Bissell found Groom Lake was not part of the proving ground, that he and Miller asked the Commission to add it, and that Chairman Lewis Strauss agreed. That is how the site got its jurisdiction. What the board declines to do is take the next step. Four guests across four Michels lead maps place the Commission at a custody point for recovered material. Nothing in either statute, and nothing in the National Archives description of Record Group 326, says anything of the kind. The node carries the statute, and the testimony stays off it.
openQuestions: Nothing in the 1946 Act, the 1954 Act or the National Archives description of Record Group 326 speaks to recovered non-nuclear material. The statute permits a custody the record does not evidence, and the board holds only the permission.

dossier.whatItIs: The civilian atomic authority of the United States from 1 August 1946 to 11 October 1974. It was created by section 2(a) of the Atomic Energy Act of 1946 as a five-member commission appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, and it took statutory title under section 9(a) to everything the Manhattan Engineer District had held: all fissionable material, all atomic weapons and parts, and such other property in the custody or control of the District as the President might determine. It ran the born-secret information regime, it seated a Division of Military Application under a serving officer of the armed forces from the beginning, and it was abolished by the Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, its functions vesting in ERDA and passing from there to the Department of Energy.
dossier.whyImplicated: Three reasons, all statutory rather than testimonial. First, it is the only body in American law that has ever held a general custody title of the kind a recovery account requires, and the language of section 9(a) is broad enough to reach property that has nothing to do with fissionable material. Second, it ran the only classification regime in the United States where secrecy attaches by operation of statute rather than by an official's decision, so that a category of information is born classified and stays that way until the Commission affirmatively releases it. Third, it is the landlord: at CIA's request in 1955 it absorbed Groom Lake into its Nevada real estate, and the strip known by its map designation as Area 51 was added to the Nevada Test Site with the President's approval. The Commission's authority is the reason the most secure aviation site in the country sits inside an atomic reservation.
